hero.tagline: A native macOS menu bar utility that temporarily locks your keyboard so you can clean it without triggering keys. The cursor keeps moving, and a palm on the trackpad scrolls and clicks nothing.
demo.caption: This is the app's own panel, rebuilt for the page: change the settings, lock it, hold Esc for three seconds to release. Nothing here touches your keyboard.
why.title: Why
why.text: Wiping crumbs out of a MacBook keyboard usually means dragging a Finder window full of garbage characters and accidentally launching apps. dirtymac suppresses every keystroke at the system event-tap level until you click stop. The cursor keeps moving the whole time, but a palm on the trackpad scrolls and clicks nothing.
why.caption: Lock from the menu bar, wipe the keys, click once to release.
features.title: Features
features.lead: Small utility, but thorough about the edge cases.
f.lock.title: One-click lock
f.lock.text: Lock and release straight from the menu bar — no window, no Dock icon.
f.shortcut.title: Global shortcut
f.shortcut.text: Open the menu bar panel from any app with ⌃⌥⌘K — change it or turn it off in Settings.
f.spotlight.title: Spotlight and Shortcuts
f.spotlight.text: Lock the keyboard or open the panel from Spotlight or the Shortcuts app — even when dirtymac isn't running.
f.keys.title: Every key, not just letters
f.keys.text: Regular keys, modifiers, and the brightness, volume, media and F-key controls are all blocked.
f.basic.title: Basic mode
f.basic.text: The cursor stays live and so does the menu bar icon: click it to release the lock. Scrolling, gestures and clicks elsewhere are ignored, and the trackpad's system swipes are switched off for the lock and put back after.
f.advanced.title: Advanced mode
f.advanced.text: Optionally freeze the mouse, trackpad and gestures too, pick which key classes to block, and set an auto-unlock timer.
f.exit.title: Always a way out
f.exit.text: Hold Esc for three seconds to release — works even in full lockdown, and finishes when you let go so no stray Esc reaches your app.
f.secure.title: Honest about Secure Input
f.secure.text: When a password field or Terminal's Secure Keyboard Entry stops macOS from letting any app block keys, dirtymac says so instead of pretending.
f.session.title: Ends with your session
f.session.text: The lock lets go when your Mac sleeps, the screen locks or users switch.
f.sound.title: Sound cues
f.sound.text: A short sound when the keyboard locks, while you hold Esc and before it unlocks — easy to turn off.
f.onboarding.title: Guided first launch
f.onboarding.text: Three-step onboarding with live Accessibility-permission status, plus a one-time What's New after each update.
f.login.title: Open at login
f.login.text: Start dirtymac with your Mac — offered during onboarding, changeable any time in Settings.
f.status.title: Live status
f.status.text: Elapsed time and auto-unlock countdown while locked. The event tap re-enables itself if macOS times it out.
f.languages.title: 17 languages
f.languages.text: Runtime language switching and a light / dark override — no relaunch needed.
f.offline.title: Nothing leaves your Mac
f.offline.text: No network access unless you turn on update checks, no analytics, no background daemons.
install.title: Install
brew.title: Homebrew (recommended)
brew.text: The cask is signed and notarized, and upgrades come through brew.
brew.note: Homebrew 6.0 and later require third-party taps to be trusted first. If you see Refusing to load cask … from untrusted tap, trust the tap once and retry:
manual.title: Manual download
manual.text: Grab the latest signed and notarized DMG, then drag dirtymac.app into /Applications.
manual.note: Both the app and the DMG carry their own stapled notarization ticket from 1.1.2 on, so the installed copy verifies with no network at all. To check your copy:
permissions.title: Permissions
permissions.p1: dirtymac needs Accessibility access to intercept keyboard events. On first launch, click the menu bar icon and choose Grant Access. macOS then prompts you to enable dirtymac in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility. Toggle it on and reopen the popover.
permissions.p2: The accessibility tap only swallows events — nothing is recorded, logged or forwarded.
how.title: How it works
how.p1: dirtymac creates a CGEventTap at the session level. The event mask is built from the active lock configuration: keyDown and keyUp are always present, while flagsChanged, the aux-control channel behind brightness / volume / media keys, and the mouse, trackpad and scroll types are added when the matching toggles are on (Ignore scrolling and clicks, and the Advanced mouse freeze). The pointer events are tapped a second time at the HID level, before the session. The callback returns nothing for blocked events, removing them from the system input queue.
how.p2: In Basic mode plain mouse movement is not in the mask, so the cursor keeps moving. Clicks, drags, scrolling and gestures are, behind a guard that lets a press through only when it goes down over one of dirtymac's own windows, which keeps the click that opens the menu and releases the lock working. Advanced full lockdown freezes the cursor too, and the universal hold-Esc exit plus a mandatory auto-unlock timer guarantee the lock can always be released. If macOS disables the tap after a timeout, dirtymac re-enables it automatically.
how.p3: On macOS 27 trackpad scrolling reaches apps without passing any event tap, and the system swipes (Mission Control, Spaces) are handled by the Dock. So during a lock dirtymac also covers every screen with a nearly invisible window of its own, below the menu bar, that takes scrolls and clicks, and switches the trackpad's gesture settings off, writing the original values down first so they come back after every lock and after a crash. The power button cannot be blocked: a press never reaches an event tap, so it still puts the Mac to sleep and ends the lock.
privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.text: dirtymac runs entirely on your Mac. It makes no network connections unless you turn on Settings → Updates → Check for updates, which is off by default. Then, once a day, it asks GitHub for the number of the latest release and nothing else: no identifier, cookie or usage data is sent, and GitHub can see your IP address like any website you visit. There is no telemetry, analytics or crash reporting, and no background process — quitting the app fully releases the keyboard. The hardened runtime is enabled. The app is unsandboxed because the system event tap requires it.
